To handle the nonlinearities in both the observation model and some state transition models as well as any noise term, we apply the Sampling Importance Resampling (SIR) particle filter with residual resampling step as detailed in Doucet et al. ( 2001 ), Arulampalam et al. ( 2002 ). In this case, target’s a priori distribution \( p\left( {{\varvec{x}}_k |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k} } \right) \) starting from \(p\left( {{\varvec{x}}_0 } \right) \) is approximated by a set of N weighted Dirac delta functions as follows: $$\begin{aligned} p\left( {{\varvec{x}}_k |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k} } \right) \approx {\mathop {\sum }\limits _{i=1}^{N}} \omega _k^i \delta \left( {{\varvec{x}}_k -{\varvec{x}}_k^i } \right) , \end{aligned}$$ (6) where \({\varvec{x}}_k^i \) is one of the N particles. The particles transit through the state transition model in SIR, while their normalized associated weights, \(\left\{ {\omega _k^i ,i=1:N} \right\} \) , are calculated based on the principle of importance sampling through the observation model and the resampling stage such that \({\mathop {\sum }\nolimits _{i=1}^{N}} \omega _k^i =1\) . In this work, the particles are points ( \({\varvec{x}}_k^i =\left[ {x,y,z} \right] _k^i )\) in Cartesian space representing target location probability, as \({\varvec{x}}\) is expressed in Cartesian coordinates ( \(n_x =3)\) . We also express our sensor state in the robot configuration space (typically a 6 or 7 dimensional space for a robotic manipulator) where the vector \({\varvec{q}}\) represents a joint angle vector ( \({\varvec{q}}_k =\left[ {q_1 ,\ldots ,q_{n_q } } \right] _k )\) . By choosing to plan sensor actions in the configuration space, we both avoid the need for robot singularity handling and feasibility checks through inverse kinematics (IK), and also facilitate joint limit avoidance by implementing them as constraints. Therefore, the observation model in ( 3 ) must bridge between these two spaces in order to update the belief state by particle filter. 4.1 Observation model The whole process of search and tracking can be handled through a particle filter as long as a thorough observation model is available. During the tracking phase a detection event represents the observation, \({\varvec{z}}_k ={\varvec{D}}_k \) , while during the searching phase, a no-detection event represents the worst-case observation scenario by considering \({\varvec{z}}_k ={\bar{{\varvec{D}}}}_k \) . As the observations in the tracking and searching phase are complementary, the detection and no-detection models are combined in a Bernoulli model to cover both cases as follows: $$\begin{aligned}&p\left( {{\varvec{z}}_k |{\varvec{x}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_k } \right) =\left[ {p\left( {{\varvec{D}}_k |{\varvec{x}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_k } \right) } \right] ^{I_1 \left( {{\varvec{x}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_k } \right) }.\nonumber \\&\quad \left[ {p\left( {{\bar{{\varvec{D}}}}_k |{\varvec{x}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_k } \right) } \right] ^{I_2 \left( {{\varvec{x}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_k } \right) }, I_i =0~or~ 1. \end{aligned}$$ (7) Here we focus on the detection model, since the no-detection model used in the searching phase is simply the complementary part. Our proposed continuous detection model, based on a pin-hole camera model, also encapsulates the depth parameter. A similar approach is considered in Ye and Tsotsos ( 1999 ) to generate a discrete geometry-based camera observation model called sensed sphere. This sensed sphere is a subsection of a sphere generated by intersecting camera view volume—defined by camera bounding planes—and concentric spheres of different radiuses centered at camera location. The observation probability is considered constant within this discretized sensed sphere which does not address both depth and boundary effects in image processing, and also can be computationally expensive to implement. To both consider the image edge effect and a nominal detection depth range as well as to bridge between the Cartesian space and configuration space, we define our heuristic detection model in the image frame, \(\mathcal{F}_i \) , considering \(\left[ {u,v,d} \right] _k \) coordinates. The image plane is a rectangular plane with poor detection capability on the edges. To encapsulate these features, we construct our detection model from the product of four sigmoid functions centered close to the edges of the image plane. When \(L_u \) and \(L_v \) represent the width in pixels of the image plane in u and v directions with a safety bound of size \(\epsilon \) , the model is expressed as follows: $$\begin{aligned}&p\left( {{\varvec{D}}_k |\left[ {u,v,d} \right] _k } \right) = \Gamma \left( {d_k } \right) .\nonumber \\&\quad {\mathop {\prod }\limits _{i=1}^{2}} \frac{1}{1+e^{\left( {-1} \right) ^{i}\alpha \left( {u_k -l_u } \right) }}.\frac{1}{1+e^{\left( {-1} \right) ^{i}\alpha \left( {v_k -l_v } \right) }},\nonumber \\&\quad l_u =\left( {-1} \right) ^{i}\left( {L_u /2-\epsilon } \right) , \nonumber \\&\quad l_{v} =\left( {-1} \right) ^{i}\left( {L_v /2-\epsilon } \right) , \end{aligned}$$ (8) where \(\alpha \) defines the slope of the sigmoid functions. In this model, \(\Gamma \left( {d_k } \right) \) is the depth coefficient to account for the depth effect in the detection model. This model is depicted in Fig. 2 a for the case when \(\Gamma \left( {d_k } \right) =1\) . The schematic representation of the overall detection model is presented in Fig. 2 b when the depth coefficient is defined as follows: $$\begin{aligned} \Gamma \left( {d_k } \right) =\frac{1}{1+e^{-\beta _s \left( {d_k -d_s } \right) }}.\frac{1}{1+e^{\beta _l \left( {d_k -d_l } \right) }}. \end{aligned}$$ (9) This coefficient is formed by the product of two sigmoid functions of depth. The first function with a sharp slope ( \(\beta _{s})\) represents the shortest range, \(d_s \) , that the object is detectable by the camera. This shortest range is usually the depth at which the entire target fits in the FoV or the target image deblurs. The second function with a mild slope ( \(\beta _{l})\) defines the longest detection range, \(d_{l}\) , at which the target is so far away that is no longer detectable. Both \(d_{s}\) and \(d_{l}\) depend on the target size, sensor specifications, lighting condition and the detection algorithm that can be calculated or experimentally examined for a given platform in model base detection algorithms. In the case of a 3D camera like the Microsoft Kinect, where the depth information is extracted from point cloud data, this information is provided by the sensor’s manufacturer. The model presented in ( 8 ) is defined in the image space, while the particles representing the target location probability are expressed in the Cartesian space. To transfer all of the particles defined in the world frame to the image frame, we consider the robot base frame, \(\mathcal{F}_b \) , as the world frame. In this case all of the points are expressed through homogenous transformation matrices \({ }_o^b \mathbf{T}\) . Here, \({ }_o^b \mathbf{T}\) , \({ }_e^b \mathbf{T}\) and \({ }_c^e \mathbf{T}\) represent transformation matrices from the object frame to the base frame, the robot end-effector frame to the base frame and the camera frame to the end-effector frame respectively. Thus, any object can be expressed in the camera frame, \({ }_o^c \mathbf{T}\) , by the following kinematic transformation: $$\begin{aligned} { }_o^c \mathbf{T}={ }_c^e \mathbf{T}^{-1}{ }_e^b \mathbf{T}^{-1}\left( {q_k } \right) { }_o^b \mathbf{T}. \end{aligned}$$ (10) Here, \({ }_c^e \mathbf{T}\) is the camera extrinsic parameters matrix captured through camera calibration, while \({ }_e^b \mathbf{T}\) is a function of the sensor state \({\varvec{q}}_k \) . Note that \({ }_e^b \mathbf{T}\) is calculated through the robot’s forward kinematics and accounts for the sensor motion model in ( 2 ) affecting the overall observation model. Therefore, any point \({\varvec{x}}_k \) at time step k expressed in the base frame \(\mathcal{F}_b \) can be expressed in the image frame \(\mathcal{F}_i \) as a function of \({\varvec{q}}_k \) as follows: (11) Here, \(\hbox {K}\) is the camera calibration matrix defined by the camera intrinsic parameters, and \(\left[ {I|0} \right] \) is a matrix formed by a 3x3 identity matrix and a zero vector. Substituting ( 11 ) and ( 9 ) into ( 8 ) provides the heuristic detection model that is a function of the target and sensor states ( \({\varvec{x}}_k \) and \({\varvec{q}}_k )\) . This detection model or its complement is then used to update the target belief state in the particle filter update stage. It is also used to form different cost functions; by substituting ( 2 ) into ( 11 ), optimal sensor control actions can be derived to make efficient observations. In the next section we develop a cost function to make efficient sensor actions in the searching phase. Therefore, the no-detection model is considered as the observation model from now on unless stated otherwise. As the target is recovered, the same procedure can be followed by adopting the detection model instead to continue with the tracking phase. 4.2 Cost function The entropy of a random variable in information theory is a measure of its uncertainty. For a continuous random variable \(\theta \) with PDF \(p\left( \theta \right) \) , the entropy is calculated as follows: $$\begin{aligned} \hbox {H}\left( {p\left( \theta \right) } \right) =-\smallint p\left( \theta \right) \log p\left( \theta \right) d\theta . \end{aligned}$$ (12) As more information becomes available, the random variable entropy reduces. Therefore, the entropy of the target belief state can provide us with a cost function in order to make informative optimal observations. As observations are collected over time, the entropy is calculated as follows: $$\begin{aligned}&\hbox {H}\left( {p\left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k+1} } \right) } \right) \nonumber \\&\quad =-\smallint p\left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k+1} } \right) \log p\left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k+1} } \right) d{\varvec{x}}_k . \end{aligned}$$ (13) Utilizing the particle filter approximation, one can substitute ( 6 ) into ( 13 ) to achieve the following approximation: $$\begin{aligned} \hbox {H}\left( {p\left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k+1} } \right) } \right) \approx -{\mathop {\sum }\limits _{i=1}^{N}} \omega _{k+1}^i \log \omega _{k+1}^i , \end{aligned}$$ (14) which is the same as the entropy of a discrete random variable. Even though the particles’ locations are not addressed in this approximation, this is a sufficient measure to reduce uncertainty of the target belief state based on the particles’ weights, as long as the weights are updated through observations. The case to account for particles’ location when the weights are not updated will be handled later when we propose our greedy planning. We also consider an additional travel distance term in the cost function to minimize the sensor action cost. This addresses the fact that, in high-DoF robotic platforms, multiple robot configurations can result in the same end-effector location, or that different observations might result in similar entropy reductions. The resulting cost function is then as follows: $$\begin{aligned} \hbox {J}\left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} ,{\varvec{q}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_{k+1} } \right)= & {} -\left( {1-\rho } \right) {\mathop {\sum } \limits _{i=1}^{N}} \omega _{k+1}^i \log \omega _{k+1}^{i}\nonumber \\&+\,\rho \left( {{\varvec{q}}_k -{\varvec{q}}_{k+1} } \right) ^{\mathrm{T}}\Phi \left( {{\varvec{q}}_k -{\varvec{q}}_{k+1} } \right) .\nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$ (15) Here \(0<\rho \le 1\) is a coefficient to adjust the emphasis on travel distance, while \(\Phi \) is a diagonal matrix assigning different positive weights to different robot joints, as they may not have equivalent travel costs. This cost function is similar to the one presented in Ramirez et al. ( 2014 ); however, we will further improve it later to account for sensor constraints and particle locations. We will also compare the performance of this cost function against the probability of detection cost function. The probability of detection cost function that we chose for comparison is the probability of no-detection when it is marginalized over all possible target states. This is the same as the normalization factor in the update formula in ( 5 ) for no-detection likelihood, and it represents the volume under the target belief state PDF after being carved by the no-detection likelihood. Considering the normalization factor in ( 5 ) in its particle filter representation and adding the travel distance term provides us with an alternative cost function as follows, similar to the one in Espinoza et al. ( 2011 ): $$\begin{aligned} \hbox {J}\left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} ,{\varvec{q}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_{k+1} } \right)= & {} \left( {1-\rho } \right) {\mathop {\sum }\limits _{i=1}^{N}} \omega _{k}^{i} p\left( {{\varvec{z}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{x}}_{k+1}^{i} ,{\varvec{q}}_{k+1}} \right) \nonumber \\&+\,\rho \left( {{\varvec{q}}_k -{\varvec{q}}_{k+1} } \right) ^{\mathrm{T}}\Phi \left( {{\varvec{q}}_k -{\varvec{q}}_{k+1}} \right) .\nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$ (16) Irrespective of the adopted cost function, the planner should be able to account for the robot motion limitations such as joint and velocity limits via constraints. These limitations and constraints are discussed in the following section. 4.3 Constraints The constraints applied in the literature are usually of simple form, such as maximum turning rate or speed in UAV and mobile robots, that are implemented in the sensor motion model. However, in the case of high-DoF robotic manipulators with nonlinear constraints of joint limits, a constraint optimization is required. To avoid complexity, we introduce a penalty function to our cost functions in ( 15 ) and ( 16 ) in the following form in order to account for the joint limits: $$\begin{aligned}&\Lambda \left( {{\varvec{q}}_k } \right) ={\mathop {\prod }\limits _{i=1}^{n_q}} \left[ {\lambda \left( {q_i } \right) } \right] _{k},\nonumber \\&\left[ {\lambda \left( {q_i } \right) } \right] _k \!=\!\left( {1+e^{-\gamma \frac{\left( {q_i -q_{imin} } \right) \left( {q_{imax} -q_i } \right) }{\left( {q_{imax} -q_{imin} } \right) ^{2}}}} \right) _k , \quad i\!=\!1,\ldots ,n_q .\nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$ (17) In this penalty function, \(q_{imin} \) and \(q_{imax} \) represent the minimum and maximum joint limits of joint i respectively. The coefficient \(\gamma \) is chosen to be a large number such that it will suddenly increase the cost close to the joint limits. This penalty function is depicted in Fig. 3 for a sample joint with joint limits of \(\left[ {-3~3} \right] ~rad\) and various \(\gamma \) . This penalty function is applied to the cost functions in ( 15 ) and ( 16 ) as follows: $$\begin{aligned} \hbox {J}_c \left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} ,{\varvec{q}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_{k+1} } \right) = \Lambda \left( {{\varvec{q}}_k } \right) .\hbox {J}\left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} ,{\varvec{q}}_k ,{\varvec{q}}_{k+1} } \right) . \end{aligned}$$ (18) Fig. 3 Full size image An example of the penalty function for a joint with joint limits of \(\left[ {\mathbf{- 3\,\, 3}} \right] ~ rad\) The same approach can be adopted to take the velocity and acceleration limits of a robotic manipulator into account. However, an alternative approach is to implement these limits in the sensor motion model in ( 2 ). In this work we implement the velocity limits as the constraints in the sensor motion model, as we manipulate our hardware through velocity control. This is provided by: $$\begin{aligned} {\varvec{q}}_{k+1} ={\varvec{q}}_k +{\varvec{u}}_k \Delta , \quad 0<\left| {{\varvec{u}}_k } \right| <{\dot{\varvec{q}}}_{max}, \end{aligned}$$ (19) where \(\Delta \) is the time step in the control loop and \(\ddot{{\varvec{q}}}_{max}\) is the robot maximum velocity vector in joint space. Substituting this equation into ( 11 ) provides us with an observation model as a function of robot velocity. This allows us to plan observations in a greedy or RHC fashion, as discussed in the next section. 4.4 Planning horizon Even though the low computational cost of greedy planning is appealing for a fast and efficient online LTS, it has the potential to get stuck in local minima (Lin et al. 2014 ). As indicated in the literature, RHC can not only ameliorate this issue; it also has other benefits in this context. For example, the navigational challenges of a UAV in a hostile environment makes RHC inevitable, as discussed in Tian et al. ( 2008 ). RHC is also helpful for cases where sensors have limited FoV or constrained footprint (Ryan and Hedrick 2010 ; Tisdale et al. 2009 ). In such systems, if the sensor location is far from the prior target distribution, a greedy search would not return an optimal solution. This is the case where the particles’ weights do not get updated, as mentioned earlier in the cost function section. This is a rare scenario in UAV search, as usually a broad prior PDF covers the entire search space based on the map, the available information of the terrain, and the lost target (Lin et al. 2014 ). In eye-in-hand systems, even if the robot has limited navigational challenges apart from joint limits, the mounted camera is a limited FoV sensor, and the lost target has narrow prior PDF based on the limited information prior to leaving the FoV. Therefore RHC is an inevitable choice, unless we address the case where the next step observation over the entire range of sensor motion does not return any information. In such a case, as depicted in Fig. 4 b, for a simplified 2D search the cost of any action is similar, and the system lacks a policy to make an action. Instead of horizon planning for such scenario, we propose a switching objective function to solve this challenge for greedy planning. Whenever the observation model does not return any new information, we switch from minimizing the belief state entropy (or probability of no-detection) in ( 18 ), to minimizing the distance between the agent and the observation location that maximizes information gain. The switching happens when the observation model does not carve out any volume from the target belief state PDF. This switch is implemented through the detection model in ( 8 ) when the observed weights of all particles for detection event return close to zero. Considering the particles’ weight vector, \({\varvec{\omega }} _k \) , and a small number \(\varepsilon \) , the switch is: $$\begin{aligned} ||{\varvec{\omega }} _k ||<\varepsilon ,\quad when \quad {\varvec{z}}_k ={\varvec{D}}_k . \end{aligned}$$ (20) When the switch happens, we propose to apply a sample-based approach that is more aligned with information gain. In fact we try to sample from \(p\left( {{\varvec{z}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k} } \right) \) when \({\varvec{z}}_k ={\varvec{D}}_k \) , that is, the future observation in one step based on all previous observations. This is the PDF that appears in the denominator of the update formula in ( 5 ) for detection likelihood: $$\begin{aligned} p\left( {{\varvec{z}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k} } \right) \!=\!{\smallint } p\left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k} } \right) p\left( {{\varvec{z}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} ,{\varvec{q}}_{k+1} } \right) d{\varvec{x}}_{k+1} .\nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$ (21) By sampling from this distribution, we are simulating a combinatorial optimization technique to find an approximate optimal sensor state \({\hat{{\varvec{q}}}}_{k+1} \) , which in turn minimizes the belief state entropy in the next step so long as the observation could happen at that state. Then we try to minimize the distance from the current sensor state \({\varvec{q}}_k \) to that configuration as it is not possible to jump from \({\varvec{q}}_k \) to \(\hat{{{\varvec{q}}}}_{k+1} \) in one step. This generates an action towards an optimal location in the future when no new sensor action in one step from \({\varvec{q}}_k \) can return new information. The distribution in ( 21 ) is formed by the propagated target state through the state transition model and the detection model. We follow the approach presented in Ryan and Hedrick ( 2010 ) to randomly sample from this distribution when the target PDF is approximated by the particle filter. The particle filter allows us to use the particle locations and weights to approximate the distribution in ( 21 ) as follows: $$\begin{aligned} p\left( {{\varvec{z}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k} } \right) ={\mathop {\sum }\limits _{i=1}^{N}} {\omega _{k}^{i}} p\left( {{\varvec{z}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{x}}_{k+1}^i } \right) . \end{aligned}$$ (22) In order to facilitate the random sampling process from ( 22 ), we need to replace the detection model with a distribution from which random sampling techniques already exist. A normal distribution in the particle’s space (Cartesian space) with mean, \(\mu ,\) and covariance, \(\sum \) , as functions of \({\varvec{x}}_{k+1}^i \) is a reasonable assumption to replace the detection model (achieved by substituting ( 11 ) into ( 8 )). The resulting multivariate Gaussian mixture model (GMM) is as follows: $$\begin{aligned} p\left( {{\varvec{z}}_{k+1} |{\varvec{z}}_{1:k} } \right) =\mathop \sum \limits _{i=1}^N \omega _k^i \mathcal{N}\left( {\mu \left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1}^i } \right) ,\sum \left( {{\varvec{x}}_{k+1}^i } \right) } \right) . \end{aligned}$$ (23) We sample \(N_s \) times ( \({\varvec{x}}_{k+1}^s , s=1:N_s )\) from this distribution, where our number of samples is much smaller than our number of particles ( \(N_s <N)\) . The number of samples is chosen by trial and error through an iterative process as explained in Ryan and Hedrick ( 2010 ). Then each sample in Cartesian space is simply associated with a camera transformation matrix, \({ }_c^b \mathbf{T}_{k+1}^s \) , based on geometry by assuming that only camera orientation should change to point at the sample position. This is a valid assumption, as long as the target is not lost due to an occlusion. These camera transformation matrices, \(\left\{ {{ }_c^b {\mathbf{T}_{k+1}^{s}}{ } ^{-1},s=1:N_s } \right\} \) , replace \({ }_c^e \mathbf{T}^{-1}{ }_e^b \mathbf{T}^{-1}\left( {{\varvec{q}}_k } \right) \) in ( 11 ) to provide simulated sample observations based on our heuristic observation model. Then the sample observation that gains maximum information (minimum entropy) results in an optimal sample point \(\hat{{x}}_{k+1} \) . $$\begin{aligned} {\hat{{\varvec{x}}}}_{k+1} ={\mathop {\hbox {argmin}}\limits _{x_{k+1}^s}} \left( -{\mathop {\sum }\limits _{i=1}^{N}} \omega _{k+1}^i \log \omega _{k+1}^{i} \right) ,~s=1:N_{s}. \end{aligned}$$ (24) Finally the \({\hat{{\varvec{x}}}}_{k+1} \) associated optimal camera transformation matrix, \({ }_c^b {\hat{\mathbf{T}}}_{k+1} \) , results in the optimal sensor state, \({\hat{q}}_{k+1} \) , through one call of IK. This approach allows us to have different target and sensor spaces while bridging between them with low computational cost. It is through this switching greedy approach that we account for particle locations in the cost function and provide a tool to avoid getting stuck in local minima. Our overall greedy LTS algorithm including the switching cost function is presented in Algorithm 1. The stage a) in Algorithm 1 uses a constrained nonlinear solver (fmincon in MATLAB) to generate optimal \({\varvec{u}}_k \) that minimizes ( 18 ). The connection between \({\varvec{u}}_k \) in ( 19 ) and ( 18 ) is built by a series of substitutions: ( 19 ) into ( 11 ), ( 11 ) into ( 8 ), ( 8 ) into ( 7 ), ( 7 ) into ( 6 ), ( 6 ) into ( 15 ), and ( 15 ) into ( 18 ). Moreover, to visualize the optimal sensor action planning process in one step when switched, we present a simplified 2D search where the target and sensor state space are the same as depicted in Fig. 4 . All of the stages are addressed in Algorithm 1 A similar approach to our switching cost function is proposed in Wong et al. ( 2005 ), where the objective function switches between the CDP, and the agent’s distance to the mode of the target PDF, when the CDP goes below a certain threshold. Their switch is the same as replacing the optimal sample in ( 24 ) with: $$\begin{aligned} {\hat{{\varvec{x}}}}_{k+1} ={\varvec{x}}_{k+1}^i ,\hbox { i}={\mathop {\hbox {argmax}}\limits _{i}} \left( {\omega _i } \right) . \end{aligned}$$ (25) This approach is interpreted as a tradeoff between detection reward along the path and the distance to the most probable place of the target. The same approach is adopted in Webb and Furukawa ( 2008 ) in the form of a multi objective function, where probability of detection and distance of the sensor from the mode of the target PDF are combined linearly. However, it is claimed that the detection objective tends to explore local areas with high probability before moving the sensor to the area of maximum probability. Navigating towards the peak of the target belief state PDF has also been applied as the only planner in the general search method in Ma et al. ( 2011 ) and is known as streaming Drosophila search (Chung and Burdick 2012 ). Another switching approach is used in Chung and Furukawa ( 2009 ) to plan greedy actions through a linear combination of a search and capture objective. When the sensor agent is far from the target, the distance between the agent and the weighted average of the particles (mean of the target belief state PDF) is minimized, and as it gets closer, the uncertainty in target state is minimized by minimizing the sum of variances on the state. This switch is the same as replacing the optimal sample in ( 24 ) with: $$\begin{aligned} {\hat{x}}_{k+1} ={\mathop {\sum }\limits _{i=1}^{N}} \omega _i x_{k+1}^{i} . \end{aligned}$$ (26) In the result section we demonstrate the benefits of using ( 24 ) instead of ( 25 ) and ( 26 ), while keeping the rest of the algorithm consistent. We believe that our approach is a more general approach as it can include both ( 25 ) and ( 26 ) as preselected samples for ( 24 ). We also compare the performance of our greedy planning using a switching cost function against a RHC method. We choose a computationally cheap method to approximate the cost function over a horizon. We simplify the information theoretic approach presented in Ryan and Hedrick ( 2010 ) as follows to reduce the computational cost and make it more suitable for an online LTS planning. Instead of constructing an approximate cost function from samples over a planning horizon \(\tau \) to plan the optimal control action, we choose the action associated with the sample with minimum cost as a worst-case (minimax) approach. We also simplify the entropy calculation to ( 14 ) instead of constructing a continuous distribution from particles for entropy measurement. Finally, we implement our proposed greedy planner to drive an efficient search on a high dimensional robotic platform. This implementation fully reveals the potential of our proposed observation model to update our knowledge of the target state in 3D Cartesian space when the sensor makes actions in 7D configuration space. It also shows rapid recovery of a lost target for visual servoing and tracking applications where online and efficient algorithms are required to keep the target in the FoV as much as possible. Simulation and experimental results and comparisons are presented in detail in the next section. 5 Results In order to compare the effect of different cost functions and of horizon planning versus greedy search, we first implement our search strategy on two of the manipulator’s wrist joints. Treating the mounted camera as a pan-tilt search platform as a result simplifies our comparisons and makes them analogous to the most common 2D search in the UAV literature. We also believe that as long as there is no occlusion, a pan-tilt search is a feasible search for online robotic vision applications. We then present improved performance by providing the results of our high dimensional search algorithm implementation. As our LTS method is not analytically tractable, we compare its various aspects through multiple repeated simulation and experimental trials for various initial conditions and present the statistically analyzed empirical results. The quality measures used for comparison depend on the simulation trial termination condition as it is handled variously in the literature (Lin et al. 2014 ). One such termination condition is that when CDP reaches a certain threshold, then the number of steps is compared as a quality measure (Bertuccelli and How 2006 ). Alternatively, a specific time is considered as another termination condition while CDPs are compared as a quality measure (Lin et al. 2014 ). We then use the number of steps as the search speed measure to compare among different methods. We also consider the travel distance of the sensor during search as a measure to account for sensor action cost. Here, the travel distance is measured by the Euclidean distance in joint space. In each set of simulation comparisons the result of 100 simulation trials are provided in this work. We also use 64 particles for the experiments presented in the following sections based on some simulation test cases and the fact that the computational cost for a particle filter increases at least linearly with number of particles. 5.1 Experimental platform To implement our proposed online high dimensional LTS algorithm, we consider a visual servoing platform incorporating in a 7-DoF robotic arm (Barrett Technology WAM) equipped with a PrimeSense Carmine 1.09 camera tracking an object tagged with an ARTag, as presented in Fig. 7 . The RGB images are only used with a model-based ARTag detection to detect and localize the target in 3D with respect to the camera. We utilize a visual servoing algorithm capable of docking to and then following a target moving at 5 cm/s. The target is mounted on a toy train moving along a stadium shaped train track with circumference of 178 cm. As the toy train’s maximum speed is about 8 cm/s, the robot cannot keep up with the target, and the target leaves the FoV. At that point our algorithm is triggered to quickly recover the target along the uneven track as quickly as possible. A similar platform is simulated where the train track can have any random shape to validate the capabilities of our system. For all experimental and simulation trials a constant acceleration state transition model is considered for \(f_{k+1} \) in ( 1 ), while a constant velocity sensor motion model is considered for \(g_{k+1} \) in ( 2 ) as indicated by ( 19 ), and \(h_k \) in ( 3 ) is derived by substituting ( 11 ) into ( 8 ) and then into ( 7 ). Here we compare each aspect of our search algorithm step by step, starting with the cost function in the next section. Here we demonstrate the common drawback of each alternative option. The shortcoming of the switch presented in ( 25 ) is evident when all the particles have the same weight, e.g., at the beginning when no observation is made. In this case any particles can represent the mode of the target PDF as depicted in Fig. 5 a, delaying the information gathering process. The drawback of the switch in ( 26 ) is when there is a bifurcation in particle distribution, in which case the target PDF mean is a local minimum that no particle gets updated on, as depicted in Fig. 5 b. On the other hand, our proposed switch in ( 24 ) that always tries to gain maximum information is a more general switch, as it can include both of the alternative switches as two hardcoded samples. The only argument against our proposed switch could be its computational cost, which is a fraction of the entire algorithm as long as ( \(N_s <N)\) . Therefore, we proceed with our proposed switch from now on. Considering our proposed switch, we compare the cost functions in a pan-tilt search for a moving target and greedy planning. We keep the robot initial configuration fixed while generating 100 random constant acceleration motion models with random initial position and velocity for the target. We keep this repository of random target motions consistent in all of our simulation evaluations. This allows us to track the effects of cost function, horizon planning, and sensor dimensionality, as presented later. The simulation results for the two cost function choices are presented in Fig. 6 a. Note that the T-bars in Fig. 6 a, as well as in the upcoming figures, represent 95 % of the range of the measured parameter given multiple (100 in this case) random initial conditions. Even though the entropy-based cost function outperforms the probability of detection cost function from the time step point of view, its travel distance is only slightly better. Comparing within each trial, the entropy-based pan-tilt greedy search has fewer time steps in 55 % of the trials and less travel distance in 39 % of the trials than the probability of detection pan-tilt greedy search. This similar performance confirms the statement in Ryan and Hedrick ( 2010 ) that in low detection probability “the maximum probability of detection has been shown to nearly solve the minimum entropy problem.” We also compare the cost functions’ performances in real experiments. In order to provide consistent and challenging conditions for comparison, we designed an experiment in which the target is intentionally occluded for a certain period of time. We placed a tunnel (depicted in Fig. 7 ) over a section of the train track, making the target suddenly invisible during tracking for about 8.1 s (65 cm) while the train was moving at around 8 cm/s. While our visual servoing algorithm tracked the target using all of the 7 DoFs, a pan-tilt search was triggered as soon as the target went into the tunnel. This experiment was conducted 40 times for each cost function, and their results are presented in Fig. 6 b. Among 40 experimental trials for each of the cost functions, 15 % of them failed and were excluded from the results in Fig. 6 b. We defined a trial failure as when the train finishes a lap without being recovered by the robot, i.e., the target would have been recovered if the robot just had waited for it to show up again without searching. However, all of the failed trials did recover the target in the train’s second lap (after the train came out of the tunnel again). Apart from the number of time steps and travel distance, we compared the actual time it took the planner to recover the target from the moment that the target left the FoV including the 8.1 s it spent under the tunnel. This comparison indicates that, even in a greedy searching phase, our robot control loop rate slowed down to about 8 Hz consistently for both cost functions, compared to about 16 Hz in the tracking phase. Finally, the experimental results presented in Fig. 6 b confirm the simulation results, namely, that both cost functions perform similarly from all measures point of view. However, we choose the entropy-based cost function for our LTS algorithm upon its slightly better performance for further evaluation in the following sections. Given our LTS problem, we can expand the search over all of the robot’s DoFs. However, in RHC this would add exponentially to the solution space and make it intractable. For example in Geyer ( 2008 ), replacing a UAV’s fixed camera with a gimbal camera is presented as a challenge, as it adds to the sensor space dimensions and requires more branching in the path optimization problem. For comparison, Fig. 10 d shows the target recovery moment by 7-DoF search where planned zooming back in addition to camera reorientation leads to target recovery. 6 Conclusion and future work In this work we discussed the problem of eye-in-hand systems as a high dimensional robotic platform actively recovering a target which leaves the camera FoV in an online manner. As robots move into more complex and unstructured environments, solving this LTS problem is highly valuable for visual tracking/servoing applications. It increases robot’s level of autonomy by providing a transition to recover a lost target as soon as possible with minimum cost. In this work we addressed this problem in a holistic manner and systematically compared it to other approaches in the literature. A novel observation model was presented to relate the space in which the target state evolves to the space in which the agent plans the search, since these two spaces can be of different types and dimensions. The problem was formulated as an optimization problem to plan fast and low cost sensor actions in higher dimensions while avoiding robot’s kinematic constraints. We believe that using the particle filter, our novel observation model, switching cost function, and greedy planning are the key steps towards online search in higher dimensions. The particle filter allows us to evolve the target belief state cheaply, suitable for higher dimensions of target space such as 3D Cartesian space. Our observation model provides the link between the target space and the robot configuration space. Our switching cost function avoids getting stuck in local minima while planning informative sensor actions considering robot’s kinematic constraints. The greedy planning approach also allows increasing the problem dimensionality with low computational cost, making it suitable for high dimensional online LTS. We then compared the performance of various features of our overall algorithm in simulation trials against other common methods to show the superior performance of our proposed algorithm. Among entropy-based pan-tilt greedy search, probability of detection pan-tilt greedy search, entropy-based pan-tilt RHC, and entropy-based 7-DoF greedy search, all of which were applied to the same 100 randomly generated simulation trials, our entropy-based 7-DoF greedy search outperformed all of the other methods. Comparing within each trial of all methods, it has fewer time steps in 72 % of the trials and less travel distance in 77 % of the trials. Real world implementation of the algorithm was also presented on an eye-in-hand visual servoing platform while servoing to and tracking a moving target. We demonstrated that our high dimensional online LTS is capable of recovering a fast moving target quickly after it leaves the FoV due to the limitations of our visual servoing algorithm. Our results also showed that a high dimensional search improves the performance, as extra DoFs provide better clearing actions. In addition, a pan-tilt search might not provide feasible views due to environmental constraints. For example, a lost target scenario caused by an occlusion cannot be handled through a pan-tilt search due to the physics of the scenario. In such scenarios, the high dimensional search should be used to reposition the camera in addition to potential reorientation through planning. Solving the optimization problem in the presence of occlusions is an interesting future work that is not addressed here. Apart from occlusions, other environmental constraints such as obstacles and self-collision are introduced challenges when planning over the entire robot’s DoFs.
